ap_chemistry-m01.stem: Which of the following hydrogen halides has the longest and weakest bond between hydrogen and the halogen?

options.why: HBr has a shorter (141 pm) and stronger (about 366 kJ/mol) H–X bond than HI (161 pm, about 299 kJ/mol), so its bond is harder to break.
HCl has a shorter (127 pm) and stronger (about 431 kJ/mol) H–X bond than HI (161 pm, about 299 kJ/mol), so its bond is harder to break.

HF has a shorter (92 pm) and stronger (about 567 kJ/mol) H–X bond than HI (161 pm, about 299 kJ/mol), so its bond is harder to break. It is also the most electronegative halogen, which makes the bond strongest rather than weakest.
Bond length grows and bond strength falls down the halogen group because the larger halogen atoms overlap less well with hydrogen; HI has the longest (161 pm) and weakest (about 299 kJ/mol) H–X bond.

stimulus.description: pH of two 100 mL solutions before and after 5.0 mL of NaOH solution is added to each

options.text: Solution A resists changes in pH because it is a more concentrated strong acid, so the added hydroxide ion is used up by a large amount of $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions.

options.text: Solution A resists changes in pH: its pH changed by only $0.03$ units while the pH of solution B changed by $8.0$ units, which shows that A contains a weak acid and its conjugate base that react with the added hydroxide ion.
options.why: A weak acid with its conjugate base neutralizes small amounts of added strong base, so the pH barely changes.

options.text: Both solutions resist changes in pH equally, because the two solutions had the same pH of $3.35$ before the NaOH was added.
options.why: Assumes equal starting pH means equal resistance to added base.

options.text: Solution B resists changes in pH: its pH changed by $8.0$ units, which is larger than the change of $0.03$ units in solution A, so B contains more dissolved particles.
options.why: Reads a larger pH change as stronger resistance to change.

ap_chemistry-m04.stem: A student measures the molar enthalpy of dissolution of an ionic compound that dissolves exothermically, using a foam-cup calorimeter. Which of the following errors would cause the calculated magnitude of the enthalpy change to be lower than the true value?

options.text: The recorded water mass is 110 g but the actual mass is 100 g.
options.why: Recording 110 g of water when only 100 g is present makes the calculated heat q = mcΔT larger, so the magnitude of ΔH is too high.

options.text: The thermometer reads the final temperature 1.0 degC too high.
options.why: A final temperature read 1.0 °C too high makes ΔT larger than the true change, so the calculated heat and the magnitude of ΔH are too high.

options.text: The salt is recorded as 5.50 g but 5.00 g is actually dissolved.
options.why: Recording 5.50 g when only 5.00 g dissolved makes the calculated moles of salt larger, so the heat per mole, and the magnitude of ΔH, is too low.

options.text: The salt is weighed and recorded as 4.50 g but 5.00 g is actually dissolved.
options.why: Recording 4.50 g when 5.00 g dissolved makes the calculated moles of salt smaller, so the heat per mole, and the magnitude of ΔH, is too high.
